title: Computing for Bioinformatics
text:
Welcome
Found a mistake, or a command that does not run for you? See Report an Issue, also linked from the bug icon at the top of the left sidebar on every page.
Computing for Bioinformatics is the computing foundation for the series Bioinformatics: A Worked Approach. It covers the Linux command line, HPC and SLURM, R and Python for everyday analysis, file formats, reproducibility (git, environments, containers), workflows (nf-core and Nextflow), and a high-level tour of the algorithms behind common tools. The other books in the series assume what is taught here.

title: Computing for Bioinformatics
text:
Who this book is for

MS and new PhD students with little computing background, mostly from biology or animal science. Engineers and computer scientists are welcome, but will find the early chapters slow.
Beginner to intermediate. You will mostly use existing tools, packages, and pipelines, not write them from scratch. Writing reusable code is covered, but it is optional and comes last.
You work, or will work, on a Linux HPC cluster (e.g., SCINet Ceres/Atlas, ISU Nova), with a laptop for editing and small analyses. Readers without cluster access can still do the local examples and read the captured cluster output.

title: Computing for Bioinformatics
section: What this book covers, and what it leaves out
text:
What this book covers, and what it leaves out
The aim is awareness, not depth. Every core tool and idea a working bioinformatician meets appears here, so that nothing in a later book is a first encounter. Each topic gets the idea, why it matters, and a hands-on use of the tool. Full algorithms (BLAST, Smith-Waterman, the FM-index, assembly graphs) are left to the book that owns them, and linked forward.
This book also owns file formats for the series: FASTA, FASTQ, SAM/BAM, BED, GFF, VCF, and friends are taught here, and other books link back.

title: Computing for Bioinformatics
text:
How to read it
Every chapter carries one label:

Core (24 chapters): work through it, with the exercises. The core chapters together are the first-pass path through the book.
Overview (8 chapters): read for understanding; no required exercises. Explains why tools behave as they do.
Optional (6 chapters): reference for later, when you need it.

Every command is marked with where it runs: your laptop, a cluster login node, or a compute node.
The book uses one software setup throughout: a pixi environment for all the tools, and VS Code as the editor, connected to a cluster by your site’s supported route. Both are set up in 2  Book setup and editors. A single running dataset, a small yeast RNA-seq experiment from the nf-core/rnaseq test data, is used from start to finish.

title: 1  Orientation: computers and where you compute
text:
1.1 What this chapter does
Core. Work through it, with the exercises.
By the end of this chapter you will have run your first commands on a real sequencing file: you will download it, check it, look inside it, and count its reads. Then we step back and look at the machine that did the work, and at the other machines you will use.
In bioinformatics, “the computer” is usually not the one in front of you. It is most often someone else’s Linux machine, such as a university or USDA cluster, that you reach from your laptop. Your laptop is still where you edit, look at results, and run small analyses. This chapter starts on the laptop, because that is where everything begins.

title: 1  Orientation: computers and where you compute
text:
1.2 Opening a terminal
Three words first. The operating system is the software that runs the computer: macOS, Windows, or Linux. The terminal is a window where you type commands. The shell is the program inside that window that reads each command, runs it, and prints the result.
Opening a terminal is the one step that really differs between systems. Pick yours; every other tabbed box on this page will follow your choice.

macOSWindows (WSL2)Linux


Open Terminal: press Cmd-SpaceCmd-Space, type Terminal, and press ReturnReturn. (It lives in Applications → Utilities.)






ImportantKey idea: switch your Mac from zsh to bash first



A new Mac’s Terminal runs zsh. Every command, output, and explanation in this book assumes bash, as on Linux and on clusters. Do all five setup steps below before the guided first session, then check that echo "$BASH_VERSION" prints 5 or higher. If you skip this, some commands and outputs will not match the book.


This book uses bash, the shell on Linux and on clusters, everywhere. A Mac needs a one-time setup to match: a new Mac’s Terminal runs a different shell (zsh), its built-in bash is version 3.2 from 2007, and its everyday tools (ls, sed, grep, …) are BSD versions whose options differ from the GNU versions on Linux (Chapter 7 explains the differences). You will install Homebrew, a package manager for macOS, use it to install a current bash and the GNU tools, and make bash your shell. Allow 15–30 minutes.

Install Homebrew. Paste the install command from brew.sh:


Terminal (laptop)

/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"

It asks for your Mac password (nothing appears as you type; that is normal) and may install Apple’s Command Line Tools first. When it finishes, it prints a Next steps section. If that section lists commands, run them: on Apple silicon Macs they let the shell find brew. Check with brew --version, which prints Homebrew’s version.
Install bash and the GNU tools.


Terminal (laptop)

brew install bash coreutils findutils gnu-sed gnu-tar grep gawk gzip

This installs a current bash; GNU coreutils (ls, wc, nproc, and about a hundred more); and GNU find, sed, tar, grep, awk, and gzip.
Make Homebrew’s bash your shell. The first line adds it to the list of allowed shells; the second switches to it. Each asks for your Mac password.


Terminal (laptop)

echo "$(brew --prefix)/bin/bash" | sudo tee -a /etc/shells
chsh -s "$(brew --prefix)/bin/bash"

Put the GNU tools first. Homebrew installs most GNU tools under names starting with g (gsed, gls), so they do not replace the Mac’s own. This command writes a small settings file, ~/.bash_profile, that bash reads each time Terminal opens. It makes brew available and puts each tool’s plain-named GNU version (sed, ls) ahead of the Mac’s. Copy all of it, from cat to the final EOF:


Terminal (laptop)

cat >> ~/.bash_profile <<'EOF'
# Homebrew, then GNU tools ahead of the macOS versions (Chapter 1)
if [ -x /opt/homebrew/bin/brew ]; then
  eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"
elif [ -x /usr/local/bin/brew ]; then
  eval "$(/usr/local/bin/brew shellenv)"
fi
for tool in coreutils findutils gnu-sed gnu-tar grep gawk; do
  PATH="$HOMEBREW_PREFIX/opt/$tool/libexec/gnubin:$PATH"
done
export PATH
# Read ~/.bashrc too, as Linux terminals do
if [ -f ~/.bashrc ]; then . ~/.bashrc; fi
EOF

Quit Terminal (Cmd-QCmd-Q), open it again, and check:


Terminal (laptop)

echo "$BASH_VERSION"
sed --version | head -n 1

5.3.15(1)-release
sed (GNU sed) 4.10
Your version numbers may be newer. If the first line starts with 3.2, step 3 did not take effect; if the second says sed: illegal option, check step 4.

From now on your Mac behaves like the Linux machines in this book.
Optional: iTerm2. Many Mac users swap Terminal for iTerm2, a free terminal app. Both run the same bash with the same settings, so every command in this book works the same in either. iTerm2 adds conveniences that help once you work on a cluster all day: one window split into several panes (say, your laptop beside a login node), search through everything a pane has printed, and a history of what you pasted. To try it, install it with brew install --cask iterm2. This book never assumes you have it.


Windows does not run the book’s commands directly. Instead you install WSL2 (Windows Subsystem for Linux), which runs a real Ubuntu Linux system inside Windows. This takes longer than on the other systems: an install, a restart, and creating a Linux account. Allow 20–30 minutes.

Open PowerShell as administrator: open the Start menu, type PowerShell, right-click Windows PowerShell, and choose Run as administrator.
Run this one command, which installs WSL2 with Ubuntu:


PowerShell (laptop, as administrator)

wsl --install

Restart Windows when it asks.
Open Ubuntu from the Start menu. The first time, it asks you to make a Linux user name and password. Nothing appears while you type the password: no dots, no stars. That is normal. Type it, press EnterEnter, and type it again.

From now on, every command in this book runs in the Ubuntu window, not in PowerShell. Its shell is bash.
If the install is blocked, your laptop may be managed by your university; ask your IT office. Microsoft’s WSL install guide has the current official steps (Microsoft 2025). You may also have heard of Git Bash; it is a different tool, and this book does not support it.


You already have a terminal. On Ubuntu, press Ctrl-Alt-TCtrl-Alt-T; on other distributions, look for Terminal in the applications menu. The shell is usually bash.









WarningPitfall: Windows folders from WSL



In WSL, keep your work in your Linux home folder (~), not under /mnt/c/..., where Linux sees your Windows files. Windows folders are slow to use from Linux and invite line-ending and permission problems (Microsoft’s advice).


Table 1.1 sums up what you now have.



Table 1.1: What you type commands into, by operating system.

The terminal shows a prompt: a short line ending in $, often with your user name and folder in front. It means “ready for a command”. Code blocks in this book leave the prompt out, so you can copy and paste them as they are. Each block is labelled with where it runs; in this chapter that is Terminal (laptop), except for the cluster box in the next section.

title: 1  Orientation: computers and where you compute
text:
1.3 Guided first session
Now run some commands. Copy each one, paste it into your terminal, press EnterEnter, and compare what you see with the output shown below it. You do not need to understand every part yet: you will learn these commands properly in Part II. Seeing them work first makes that easier.






TipPasting into a terminal



Paste with Cmd-VCmd-V on macOS and Ctrl-Shift-VCtrl-Shift-V in most Linux and WSL terminals. In a terminal, Ctrl-CCtrl-C does not copy: it stops the running command.


The file we use is a FASTQ file, the standard format for sequencing reads: each read’s bases, plus a quality score for every base. It holds yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) RNA-seq reads from an experiment by Wu et al. (2018), cut down to 50,000 reads for testing by nf-core, a community collection of bioinformatics pipelines. It is the running dataset of this book; its source and license are listed in the book’s data/README.md.






WarningPitfall: on a cluster, never on the login node



This session is meant for your laptop. If you do it on a cluster instead (say, you already have an account), do not run it on the login node, the machine you land on when you log in. Ask the scheduler for a compute node first, and run everything there, downloads included:


Terminal (login node)

srun --cpus-per-task=1 --mem=4G --time=01:00:00 --pty bash -l

This asks for 1 core, 4 GB of RAM, and 1 hour, and opens a shell on a compute node once they are free; it may take a moment. Run hostname: it should now print a different machine’s name than before. Do steps 1–6 there, then type exit to give the compute node back and return to the login node.
Many sites need more options, such as an account (-A) or a partition (-p); SCINet, for example, requires -A. Your site’s are in Appendix A. If curl cannot connect from a compute node, your site may block the internet there; ask your research computing office where to download. Chapter 10 explains all of this properly.


Step 1. Make a scratch folder and move into it.


Terminal (laptop)

mkdir -p ~/bioinf-ch01 && cd ~/bioinf-ch01

This prints nothing. In the shell, silence usually means success.
Step 2. Download one FASTQ file.


Terminal (laptop)

curl -fLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/test-datasets/rnaseq/testdata/GSE110004/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz

curl shows a progress table while it works. When it finishes, the last line starts with 100; your speeds and times will differ:
  % Total    % Received % Xferd  Average Speed   Time    Time     Time  Current
                                 Dload  Upload   Total   Spent    Left  Speed
100 2186k  100 2186k    0     0  4146k      0 --:--:-- --:--:-- --:--:-- 4141k
If instead you see curl: (56) The requested URL returned error: 404, or any other curl: error, check that you copied the whole command. If a firewall blocks curl, download the file in your browser from its GitHub page (the Download raw file button), then move it into place:

macOSWindows (WSL2)Linux




Terminal (laptop)

mv ~/Downloads/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz ~/bioinf-ch01/



Replace <your-windows-name> with your Windows user name.


Terminal (laptop)

cp /mnt/c/Users/<your-windows-name>/Downloads/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz ~/bioinf-ch01/





Terminal (laptop)

mv ~/Downloads/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz ~/bioinf-ch01/




Step 3. Check that the file arrived intact. First its size:


Terminal (laptop)

ls -lh SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz

-rw-r--r-- 1 you you 2.2M Nov 13 11:52 SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
Your name, group, and date will differ. 2.2M means about 2.2 megabytes; the next section says exactly what M counts. Then test the compression:


Terminal (laptop)

gzip -t SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz

This prints nothing if the file is intact. A damaged or incomplete download prints an error instead.
Step 4. Look at the first two reads. The file is compressed (.gz), so we decompress it on the fly and show only its first 8 lines:


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | head -n 8

@SRR6357070.25017281 25017281/1 kraken:taxid|4932
CCTGAATCGAGAAGGAGGTGTCCAGGGAGTTCATCATCAGAATGATTAGTATGATTTACTGTAGATTCAGTAAGTTTCTGGCCTAAGATGAAGGTCGTGCT
+
BBBBBFFFFFFFBFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFBFFFBFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFBFFBFFFFFFF
@SRR6357070.6710070 6710070/1 kraken:taxid|4932
GTCAGATTGGAAGTCATGGTCAGATTCTATGTTAAGATCATCGGATTGTTGGATCTCATTTGACGCAATGAACGATTGATATGAAGCAGTTAAACGGTTTA
+
BBBBBFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFB
We use gunzip -c because it works the same on every system. (You may see zcat elsewhere; the zcat built into macOS does not read .gz files.)
Step 5. Count the lines.


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | wc -l

200000
Step 6. Count the reads and save the result. Each read in this file takes four lines, as you saw in step 4, so 200,000 lines are 200,000 / 4 = 50,000 reads. This command does the same count, divides by 4, and writes one line to a file:


Terminal (laptop)

1echo "SRR6357070_1 reads: $(( $(gunzip -c SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | wc -l) / 4 ))" > fastq_summary.txt
2cat fastq_summary.txt


1

$( ... ) runs the line count from step 5 and puts its result here; $(( ... / 4 )) divides it by 4; echo prints the sentence; and > sends that sentence into the file fastq_summary.txt instead of the screen.

2

cat prints the file, so you can check what was saved.


SRR6357070_1 reads: 50000






WarningPitfall: stop at the first error



If any step prints an error, stop and fix it before going on. In particular, a summary that says reads: 0 means the download failed or the file is broken; the command still “succeeds”, because the shell does not stop on errors unless told to (Chapter 8).


You now have a one-line summary of a real sequencing file. Before moving on, look at what a read is. Figure 1.1 labels the first record from step 4.




  The first record of the file SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz, four lines long. Line 1 is the header: it starts with @, then the read ID SRR6357070.25017281, and ends its second word with /1, meaning this read is read 1 of a pair. Line 2 is the 101 bases of the read, shown cut short. Line 3 is a plus sign that separates the bases from their qualities. Line 4 holds one quality character for each of the 101 bases.
  
  
  
  
    1 · Header
    2 · Bases
    3 · Separator
    4 · Qualities
  
  
  
    read ID
    /1 = read 1 of the pair
  
  
    
    
  
  
  @SRR6357070.25017281 25017281/1 kraken:taxid|4932
  Starts with @. The rest of the header is explained in Chapter 15.
  
  CCTGAATCGAGAAGGAGGTGTCCAGGGAGTTCATCATCAG…
  The read itself: 101 bases (A, C, G, T; N if unknown), shown cut short.
  
  +
  Separates the bases from their qualities.
  
  BBBBBFFFFFFFBFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF…
  One character per base, 101 in all. B and F are both high scores.




Figure 1.1: The first record of SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz. In this file every read takes exactly four lines: a header with the read ID, the bases, a + separator, and one quality character per base. The full format, including files that break the four-line pattern, is in Chapter 15.



~/bioinf-ch01 is a scratch folder: you can delete it whenever you like. Chapter 3 starts the book’s real project and brings this file, and the address you downloaded it from, into it.

Check yourself. This FASTQ file has 200,000 lines. How many reads does it hold?






TipAnswer





50,000. In this file each read takes four lines, so 200,000 / 4 = 50,000.

text:
1.4 Parts of a computer that matter for analysis
Start with your own computer. Run the commands for your system and write your values in the last column of Table 1.2.



Table 1.2: The resources of one computer. macOS has no free, so it uses a different command for RAM; all commands are in the tabs below. The example values are from one laptop (a Mac); yours will differ.












Resource
Command (Linux / WSL)
Read this
Example output
Your value




Logical CPUs
nproc
the number
16



RAM
free -h
total in the Mem: row
64 GiB



Free disk
df -h ~
the Avail column
744G








macOSWindows (WSL2)Linux




Terminal (laptop)

nproc
echo "$(( $(sysctl -n hw.memsize) / 1073741824 )) GiB"
df -h ~

16
64 GiB
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/disk1s4s1  1.9T  1.1T  744G  61% /
nproc comes with the GNU tools you installed. The second line asks macOS for its memory in bytes and divides by 1,073,741,824 (230), giving GiB as free -h does on Linux. Read free disk from the Avail column. On a Mac, Used and Avail need not add up to Size, because several volumes share one disk.




Terminal (laptop)

nproc
free -h
df -h ~

For RAM, read the total column of the Mem: row of free -h; for disk, the Avail column of df -h ~. WSL sees only the memory Windows gives its virtual machine, by default about half the laptop’s RAM, not the full amount (WSL settings).




Terminal (laptop)

nproc
free -h
df -h ~

For RAM, read the total column of the Mem: row of free -h; for disk, the Avail column of df -h ~.



These three numbers describe the parts in Figure 1.2:

CPU (central processing unit): the part that computes. It has several physical cores, each able to work on its own. On many Intel and AMD processors, each core appears to the system as two logical CPUs; the commands above count logical CPUs. (The example laptop has 8 physical cores and 16 logical CPUs.) A running program splits its work into threads, pieces of work that the system places onto CPUs. Many tools take an option that sets how many threads to use: --threads, -t, or -p, depending on the tool. More threads help only if the tool is written to use them.
RAM (memory): the fast working space a program uses while it runs. It is emptied when the program stops.
Disk (storage): slow, large, and permanent; it keeps your files. A file’s size on disk is not the RAM a program needs to read it. The count in step 6 streams through the file a few lines at a time and needs almost no memory, whatever the file’s size. Other tools, such as those that build a genome index (Chapter 31), hold a lot in memory at once.
I/O (input/output): reading and writing files, over the disk or the network. Simple steps over big files, such as copying them or counting their lines, often spend most of their time waiting for I/O. Heavier steps, such as aligning reads, are often limited by the CPU, and some by RAM.
GPU (graphics processing unit): a separate processor with thousands of small cores, built to do the same arithmetic on lots of data at once. Most tools in this book do not use one. Where you will meet GPUs: nanopore basecalling (Dorado), deep-learning models, and GPU versions of standard tools such as BWA-MEM, STAR, and DeepVariant (NVIDIA Parabricks). Clusters usually have a few GPU nodes, which you must ask the scheduler for. Chapter 37 covers them.





  The parts of a computer that matter for analysis, from fastest to slowest: the CPU, whose cores do the work; RAM, the working space, at about 10 to 50 gigabytes per second; the local disk, which keeps files, at about 0.5 to 5 gigabytes per second for a solid-state drive; and the network, which reaches other machines and shared storage, at about 0.1 to 1 gigabyte per second. In this example the job is limited by input and output: blocks of a blue FASTQ file move slowly from disk into RAM while the CPU's cores wait.

Figure 1.2: The parts of a computer that matter for analysis, fastest on the left. Speeds are typical laptop values, order of magnitude only. Shown is one example, an I/O-limited job: blocks of the file crawl from disk into RAM while the CPU’s cores wait.



Figure 1.3 shows what threads do, and do not do, on a computer with 8 cores.

Figure 1.3: Threads on a computer with 8 cores. Left: a tool written to use threads, run with 4, keeps 4 cores busy. Right: a single-threaded step keeps 1 core busy and leaves 7 idle; asking it for more threads changes nothing.



Whether code can use more than one core also depends on the language it is written in and the packages it uses (Table 1.3). Some packages use several processes (separate copies of a running program) instead of threads. The cores fill up the same way, but each process needs its own memory.



Table 1.3: Using more than one core, by language. Brief; Chapter 12 and Chapter 13 show how, and Chapter 35 goes further.










Language
Out of the box
Ways to use more cores




R
One core: R runs one step at a time
data.table (threads; by default half your logical CPUs); the parallel package (mclapply starts extra processes; not on Windows); matrix maths, if R uses a multi-threaded BLAS library such as OpenBLAS


Python
One thread runs Python code at a time, because of the global interpreter lock (GIL)
multiprocessing and concurrent.futures (processes); NumPy matrix maths (a multi-threaded BLAS); Polars (threads on all cores). A separate free-threaded build without the GIL (e.g., python3.14t) was experimental in 3.13 and is officially supported since 3.14, but it is not the default


Julia
One worker thread, unless you ask for more
Start with julia --threads auto, then use Threads.@threads loops


C, C++, Java
Real threads, if the program is written to use them
Most heavy bioinformatics tools are written in these (samtools, BWA, and STAR in C or C++; GATK in Java). That is why they take a --threads option












CautionMisconception: “More cores always makes it faster”



Reality. Only steps written to use several threads get faster, and only until something else limits them. Many steps use one core, and some are limited by disk, network, or memory rather than the CPU.


Each resource fails in its own way when it runs out (Table 1.4). You will meet these messages; recognising them saves hours.



Table 1.4: What it looks like when each resource runs out.










Resource
What runs out
What you see




RAM
Working space while the program runs
The program stops with Killed or an “out of memory” message, often with no output file


Disk
Space to write files
No space left on device


CPU
Computing power
The job is slow; its cores show 100% busy


I/O
Speed of reading and writing
The job is slow, but its cores are mostly idle












ImportantKey idea



A job can be limited by CPU, RAM, disk space, or I/O. Extra cores help only when the work can use them.


Finding which one limits a real job is part of Chapter 10 (on a cluster) and Chapter 35.

Check yourself. A step keeps one core at 100% while seven sit idle. Will rerunning it with --threads 8 make it faster?






TipAnswer





Only if the tool supports threads. Many steps use one core whatever you ask for, and then nothing changes. Some are limited by disk or memory, not the CPU, and more threads will not help those either.

text:
1.5 How big is the data?
Start with your own file. Our sample was sequenced paired-end: each fragment of RNA (copied to DNA) was read from both ends, so the sample has two mate files, one for read 1 (_1) and one for read 2 (_2). Your file is the read-1 file. It holds 50,000 reads and takes 2.2 MB compressed (12.8 MB uncompressed). A typical RNA-seq sample has around 30 million reads in each mate file, 600 times as many. If those reads are like ours, the file is about 600 times larger:

compressed: 2.2 MB × 600 ≈ 1.3 GB
uncompressed: 12.8 MB × 600 ≈ 7.7 GB

A paired-end sample has two such files. Ours does too: your file holds 50,000 reads, and its mate file SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz holds another 50,000, so the sample is 50,000 read pairs (100,000 reads).
This kind of scaling works only for the same kind of file. Read length, header style, and compression all change the result, so treat it as an estimate.
A note on units: in this book, 1 MB is 1,000,000 bytes and 1 GB is 1,000,000,000 bytes. Some tools count in powers of 2 instead (1 MiB = 1,048,576 bytes) and often still print M. ls -lh is one of them: your 2,239,317-byte file is 2.14 MiB, which GNU ls rounds up to 2.2M. (The ls built into macOS rounds to 2.1M.) Memory is sold in binary units too: a laptop sold with “64 GB” has 64 GiB.
An analysis pipeline is a fixed series of steps run in order; for RNA-seq, roughly: align the reads (find where each one came from in the genome), count the reads on each gene, and test which genes differ between groups. Part VI shows how to run whole pipelines. The files along the way fall into two groups (Table 1.5, Figure 1.4):

Read-level files (FASTQ, BAM) hold every read: gigabytes per sample in a real study. A BAM file holds the same reads after aligning, each with its place on the genome, and is often about as large as the compressed FASTQ files it came from, sometimes larger. Sorting it into genome order needs temporary disk space on top (samtools sort).
Summary files (count matrix, results table, and in DNA studies often a VCF of variants) hold one row per gene or variant: megabytes or less for RNA-seq, small enough for any laptop.





Table 1.5: File sizes in an RNA-seq analysis. The yeast test set is measured; it uses only yeast chromosome I, which is why it has 124 genes. A whole yeast genome has about 6,000 genes and a mammal 20,000 or more. The typical study column is a rough order of magnitude.

The sample is WT_REP2, one paired run like yours (50,000 read pairs). The BAM is the nf-core/rnaseq output stored with the test data; the count matrix and results table were made from those BAMs by scripts/ch01_file_sizes.R. Read-level files are hundreds to thousands of times larger than summary files.









ImportantKey idea



Read-level files (FASTQ, BAM) are large; summary files (count matrices, results tables) are usually far smaller. Intermediate and temporary files raise the peak disk space a pipeline needs.



Check yourself. Our mate file holds 50,000 reads in 2.2 MB. About how large is a mate file of the same kind with 30 million reads?






TipAnswer





About 1.3 GB compressed: 30 million is 600 × 50,000, and 600 × 2.2 MB ≈ 1.3 GB. A paired sample has two such files.

title: 1  Orientation: computers and where you compute
text:
1.6 Why Linux
Almost every cluster runs Linux, and most bioinformatics tools are written for it first. That is why this book teaches Linux commands. macOS is close enough that nearly all of them work unchanged, and WSL gives Windows a real Linux system. Where macOS or Windows differ, the book says so.






NoteBackground: Linux distributions



Linux comes in distributions that share the same core and commands but differ in how software is installed. You will most often meet Ubuntu on laptops and WSL, and Red Hat Enterprise Linux or Rocky Linux on clusters.

section: 1.7 Where you compute: laptop, cluster, cloud
text:
1.7 Where you compute: laptop, cluster, cloud
You will use up to three kinds of computer (Table 1.6).



Table 1.6: Three places to compute.












Laptop
Cluster (HPC)
Cloud




Cost to you
already paid for
usually free or cheap through your institution
pay for each hour used and each GB stored


Size
a few to ~16 cores; 8–64 GiB of RAM
thousands of cores; nodes with hundreds of GB of RAM
as large as you pay for


Who manages it
you
research computing staff
you, on the provider’s machines


What to run there
editing, plots, R and Python on summary files, small tests
alignment, many samples, pipelines, large-memory jobs
work your cluster cannot do, or when you have no cluster






A cluster, or HPC (high-performance computing) system, is many computers, called nodes, shared by many people (Figure 1.5). You connect from your laptop to a login node with ssh (secure shell, the standard way to log in to another computer). There you edit files and submit jobs: requests for some cores, memory, and time. A program called the scheduler (on most clusters, including SCINet and Nova, SLURM) holds each job in a queue until those resources are free, then runs it on a compute node. Your files sit on shared storage, which both the login node and the compute nodes can read. Chapter 9 covers connecting and Chapter 10 the scheduler.




  The parts of an HPC cluster. Your laptop connects over SSH to a login node, where you edit files and submit jobs. Submitted jobs wait in the queue of the scheduler, SLURM on most clusters, until it starts them on compute nodes, where the work runs. Shared storage holding your data is part of the cluster and is connected to both the login node and the compute nodes; files do not pass through the scheduler. The laptop reaches the cluster only through the SSH connection and file transfers.

Figure 1.5: The parts of an HPC cluster. You reach the login node from your laptop with ssh; work runs on compute nodes when the scheduler (SLURM) starts it; shared storage is connected to both. Files do not pass through the scheduler.









CautionMisconception: “The cluster is just a faster computer”



Reality. A cluster is many ordinary computers shared by many people. You ask a scheduler for cores, memory, and time, and your job waits in a queue until they are free. A single step is often no faster than on a laptop; the gain is running many steps at once, with more memory.








WarningPitfall: heavy work on the login node



The login node is a shared doorway. Running an analysis there slows it for everyone, and many sites kill long-running processes on it. Run work on a compute node instead: interactively with srun (the box in Section 1.3), or as a submitted job (Chapter 10).


The cloud is computers you rent by the hour from a company. It costs money for every hour and every gigabyte, so for most readers it is the option for when a cluster cannot do the job. Chapter 38 introduces it.

Check yourself. Laptop, cluster, or cloud?

Editing an analysis script.
Aligning the reads of 48 samples.
Running DESeq2 (an R package that finds genes whose expression differs between groups) on this book’s small yeast count matrix.
A one-off job that needs 2 TB of RAM, more than any node of your cluster has.







TipAnswer






Laptop (or the login node, if the script lives on the cluster).
Cluster compute nodes, submitted as jobs.
Laptop: the matrix is a few kilobytes.
The cloud is one option if you have funding for it; another is a shared facility that has such nodes.

title: 1  Orientation: computers and where you compute
text:
1.8 Getting a cluster account
Most readers will need a cluster account for the later chapters. Apply early, since approval can take days or weeks. Ask your PI or your institution’s research computing office which cluster you can use.






TipApply for an account now



ARS scientists and their collaborators can sign up for SCINet, USDA’s clusters. Universities run their own, such as Iowa State’s HPC clusters (Nova). Step-by-step details are in Appendix A.


No cluster yet? Keep going: everything before Chapter 9 runs on your laptop.

title: 1  Orientation: computers and where you compute
text:
1.9 Summary

A terminal runs a shell; this book uses bash on every system (on a Mac, after installing it with Homebrew). You type commands, and code blocks in this book leave out the prompt and say where they run.
You downloaded a FASTQ file, checked it, looked at its records, and saved a read count: SRR6357070_1 reads: 50000.
Your computer’s logical CPUs, RAM, and free disk are three commands away; a job can be limited by CPU, RAM, disk, or I/O, and more threads help only tools written to use them.
Read-level files (FASTQ, BAM) are large; summary files (count matrices, results) are small. File size scales with read count for files of the same kind.
Edit and run small analyses on a laptop; run heavy jobs on cluster compute nodes, never on the login node; rent the cloud when neither will do.

title: 1  Orientation: computers and where you compute
text:
1.10 Exercises
Do these where you did the guided session: on your laptop, or, on a cluster, inside an srun session on a compute node (see the pitfall box in Section 1.3), never on the login node.

Exercise 1. Read 2. Download the matching read-2 file and add its count as a second line of fastq_summary.txt:


Terminal (laptop)

curl -fLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/test-datasets/rnaseq/testdata/GSE110004/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
echo "SRR6357070_2 reads: $(( $(gunzip -c SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz | wc -l) / 4 ))" >> fastq_summary.txt
cat fastq_summary.txt

The only change from step 6 is >> instead of >: > replaces a file’s contents, >> adds to the end (Chapter 6). Do both files have the same count? Why should they?






TipAnswer





SRR6357070_1 reads: 50000
SRR6357070_2 reads: 50000
Yes. In a paired-end run each fragment is read from both ends, so read 1 and read 2 of a pair sit at the same position in the two files, and the counts must match. Equal counts do not by themselves prove that the pairs line up; Chapter 15 shows how to check.





Exercise 2. Would it fit? Fill in your column of Table 1.2. Would an uncompressed 30-million-read mate file (about 7.7 GB) fit in your RAM if a program loaded all of it at once, leaving room for the system and your other programs?






TipAnswer





It depends on your laptop: with 8 GB of RAM, no; with 32 GB, yes. But the count from step 6 never loads the file: it streams through it, so it works on any laptop. Some tools do need that much memory or more, which is one reason to use a cluster.





Exercise 3. How long would it take? Time the line count:


Terminal (laptop)

time gunzip -c SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | wc -l

Find the elapsed time: the real line of the output. Estimate the time for a 30-million-read mate file (600 times larger), then name two reasons the real time could differ from your estimate.






TipAnswer





On the example laptop the count took 0.03 seconds, so 600 times that is about 20 seconds. Two reasons it could differ: for a file this small, the time is mostly spent starting the programs, and the file may already be in memory from step 5, so the small run is not a fair sample. And a big file may sit on a slower disk or a network filesystem, which makes reading it the limit. Measuring what limits a job is part of Chapter 10 and Chapter 35.

title: Report an Issue
text:
Which route for what
A computing book goes wrong in more ways than most: a command that worked last year fails with a new tool version, a cluster behaves differently from the one the book was tested on, a download link moves, an install breaks on one operating system. The fastest way to find these is readers. Every report is read, and the fix goes onto the website as soon as it is made.
There is no errata list. When something is wrong it is corrected in the book itself.
Issues and Discussions are kept separate on purpose. The issue tracker holds only things with a fix, so it reads as a to-do list and you can search it to see whether your problem is already reported. Questions go to Discussions because a question is not a defect, but a run of questions on the same section is a sign the explanation failed, and that does become an issue.

title: Report an Issue
text:
You have found
Use




A wrong command, output, or claim
An issue, using the Error in the book form


A command or install that fails for you (pixi, VS Code, a tool, a cluster step)
An issue, using the Something doesn’t run form


A broken link, moved download, or outdated tool version
An issue, using the Error in the book form


A typo or awkward sentence you are willing to fix
A pull request (see below)


A typo you would rather just report
The Error in the book form


A section you did not follow, or are not sure is right
A question in Discussions › Q&A


A suggestion: a better example, a missing topic or tool
An idea in Discussions › Ideas


Something that should not be public
Email the author (the address on the GitHub profile)

title: Report an Issue
text:
Before you report
Note the page. Copy the URL of the page and the section heading. The book changes often while it is being written, so say roughly when you read it.
Search the open issues. If someone has already reported it, add a comment there rather than opening a second one. A second report on the same problem is still useful: it says how many readers it affects.

title: Report an Issue
text:
Reporting an error
You need a free GitHub account. The Error in the book form asks for:

Chapter and section, with the command, code chunk, table, or figure if there is one.
What is wrong (quote it as it appears) and what it should be.
How you know. Optional, and the most useful field: the command you ran and its output, or a link to the tool’s documentation.

title: Report an Issue
text:
Reporting something that doesn’t run
Problems with installs and commands are the most common reports, and the hardest to fix without details. The Something doesn’t run form asks for:

Where you ran it: laptop, cluster login node, or compute node; the operating system (macOS, Windows with WSL2, or Linux); the cluster name if there is one (e.g., SCINet Ceres, ISU Nova).
The exact command, copied, not retyped.
The complete error message, copied as text, not a screenshot, and not shortened. The useful line is often the first error, not the last.
Your environment: the output of pixi info run in the book’s folder. On a cluster, also any module load lines you ran first.







WarningPitfall



Never paste passwords, SSH private keys, access tokens, or private data into an issue. Issues are public and stay public. Replace usernames, paths, and hostnames you would rather not share with placeholders such as <user>.

title: Report an Issue
text:
Fixing it yourself
For a typo or a wording fix, the fastest route is to make the change and propose it on GitHub:

Open the page’s source file in the repository. Chapters live in chapters/, one .qmd file each (Markdown with code), named by number: chapter 5 is chapters/05-shell-basics.qmd.
Click the pencil icon. GitHub offers to fork the repository into your own account; accept.
Make the change, write one line saying what it is, and choose Propose changes, then Create pull request.

The author reviews it, and merges it or asks for a change. Some things to know before you edit:

Edit the .qmd only. _book/ is generated output.
One fix per pull request. A three-line change is reviewed in a minute; a change that touches four chapters waits.
Do not add to references.bib unless you have checked the DOI. Every entry in it has been verified.
Your contribution is offered under the book’s licenses: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 for text and figures, MIT for code.
Larger changes (a rewritten section, a new example) should start as a discussion in Ideas, so the shape is agreed before the work is done.

title: Report an Issue
section: Asking a question or suggesting something
text:
Asking a question or suggesting something
Discussions › Q&A is for “I did not follow this step” or “is this right?”. Other readers can answer as well as the author, and an answered question stays there for the next person.
Discussions › Ideas is for a different example, a tool the book should cover, or a better way to explain something. Scope is the author’s call: this book aims for awareness, not depth, and full algorithms belong to the other books in the series. The discussion is where the case is made.

title: Report an Issue
text:
What happens next
A report is labelled with its chapter and its type (error, typo, doesnt-run, link). The fix is made on the main branch and the website updates from it. If a problem only affects one operating system or cluster, the fix may be a note in the chapter rather than a change to the command.
